Pricing & Discount Strategy Analysis

The average list price is ₹5,445, discounted to ₹3,125 on average — a 47.7% markdown. But does heavier discounting yield happier customers?

Discount % vs. Customer Rating

Correlation: r = -0.155. The relationship between discount depth and rating is weakly negative. Deeper discounts do not translate into higher customer satisfaction — they may even be associated with lower-quality products.

Discount % vs. Review Volume

Correlation: r = 0.012. The link between discounts and review volume is also weak. Heavy discounting does not meaningfully drive more customer reviews.

Review Sentiment Snapshot

A keyword-frequency analysis of review titles and content reveals the most common positive and negative themes across the catalog.

Positive themes: Customers most frequently praise quality, value, good, and nice. Words like fast and recommend indicate satisfaction with delivery/performance and willingness to endorse.
Negative themes: Common complaints center on return/refund, waste, cheap, and damage. Products receiving negative feedback often have quality or durability issues, not just pricing concerns.

Strategic Recommendations

1. Rethink Deep-Discount Strategy

With a discount-to-rating correlation of just r = -0.155, aggressive discounting is not driving satisfaction. Products in the 0–20% discount range average a rating of 4.17 — often higher than heavily discounted products. Reallocate promotional spend toward quality improvements or targeted, time-limited promotions rather than blanket deep discounts.

2. Prioritize Quality in Bottom-Performing Categories

Categories like Car&Motorbike (3.80), MusicalInstruments (3.90), Health&PersonalCare (4.00) underperform on ratings. Conduct supplier quality audits and tighten listing standards in these segments. A focused quality push could lift ratings by 0.2–0.3 points, improving category perception and conversion rates.

3. Amplify Review Generation for Mid-Tier Products

The median product has only 5,179 reviews while top-engaged products exceed 100K. Implement post-purchase review prompts and incentive programs for products in the 1K–5K review range to build social proof and close the engagement gap.

4. Invest in Premium Segments

Products priced ₹5K+ show stronger ratings, suggesting customers associate quality with price. Expand curated premium assortments in top-performing categories and market them on quality rather than discount.

5. Address Durability and Return Complaints

Negative review keywords (return, refund, waste, damage, cheap) reveal durability and build-quality as primary pain points. Partner with suppliers to improve packaging, materials, and QC — especially in categories with high review volume but lower-than-average ratings.
